The full-support manuscript proves that an admissible integrable minimizer
of the zero-temperature Parisi functional for the pure zero-field
Sherrington–Kirkpatrick model has Stieltjes support equal to every overlap
scale in [0,1). The proof turns a hypothetical support gap into a constant
interval for the order parameter. Variational contact at the ends of that
interval conflicts with a strict curvature inequality inside it. Along the
auxiliary diffusion, the spatial gradient of the value function is a bounded
martingale. Full support makes this martingale's second moment equal to time;
its terminal correlation with Brownian motion gives the ground-state value.
The manuscript's further argument gives a smooth Stieltjes density, strictly
positive on $(0,1)$, and no atom at zero. Sections 9.1–9.2 derive this stronger
ordinary conclusion separately from the selected formal support statement.

This record reconstructs those arguments and follows the finite Gaussian
approximation into the separate QAOA manuscript. The latter claims that
finite deterministic circuits approach the SK optimum when system size tends
to infinity before circuit depth increases. Its circuit construction needs
additional approximation, synthesis, seed-removal and transfer arguments.
The two formal statements concern full support and scalar value
consequences; neither states QAOA circuit convergence. Their verification
scope is described at the end. See [OpenAI (2026a), §§1–2][fs-main] and
[OpenAI (2026b), Theorem 1.1][q-intro].

For independent standard Gaussian couplings $J_{ij}$, put

$$
H_n(\sigma)=\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i<j}J_{ij}\sigma_i\sigma_j,\qquad
\sigma\in\{-1,1\}^n,\qquad
P_*=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\mathbb E\max_\sigma H_n(\sigma).
$$

For overlap $R_{12}=n^{-1}\sum_i\sigma_i^1\sigma_i^2$, the covariance is
$nR_{12}^2/2-1/2$. Thus the convention is $\xi(t)=t^2/2$, with
$\xi''=1$. A centered Gaussian of variance $1/2$, common to all
configurations, removes the final constant without changing the expected
maximum. Every normalization below uses this convention.

Let $\mathcal U$ consist of nonnegative, nondecreasing, right-continuous
functions $\gamma:[0,1)\to[0,\infty)$ with
$\int_0^1\gamma(t)\,dt<\infty$. Their Stieltjes measures satisfy
$\mu_\gamma([0,t])=\gamma(t)$, including
$\mu_\gamma(\{0\})=\gamma(0)$. They are locally finite, but need not be
probability measures or have finite total mass. Support is relative to [0,1).

Let $B$ be standard Brownian motion. The control value and Parisi
functional are

$$
\Phi_\gamma(t,x)=\sup_{|\alpha|\le1}\mathbb E\left[
 \left|x+B_1-B_t+\int_t^1\gamma(s)\alpha_s\,ds\right|
 -\frac12\int_t^1\gamma(s)\alpha_s^2\,ds\right],
$$
$$
\mathcal P(\gamma)=\Phi_\gamma(0,0)-\frac12\int_0^1t\gamma(t)\,dt.
$$

Controls are progressively measurable for Brownian increments after $t$.
For a general admissible coefficient, the solution and its spatial derivatives
are locally absolutely continuous in time on compact strips; the time equation
holds almost everywhere. The control formula fixes the solution. The PDE is
$\Phi_t=-\tfrac12(\Phi_{xx}+\gamma\Phi_x^2)$, with
$\Phi(1,x)=|x|$. Auffinger and Chen's zero-temperature Parisi formula and
attainment identify $P_*$ with $\min_{\gamma\in\mathcal U}\mathcal P(\gamma)$.
The support theorem itself assumes a minimizer and proves a property of it;
it does not separately supply one. See [OpenAI (2026a), §§1–2][fs-main]
and [Auffinger and Chen (2017), Theorem 1 and proof of Lemma 3][ac2017].

Write $u=\Phi_x$, $a=\Phi_{xx}$, and
$dX_t=\gamma(t)u(t,X_t)\,dt+dB_t$, $X_0=0$.
Write $q(t)=\mathbb E[u(t,X_t)^2]$ for the second moment of this
gradient along $X$.
The first result assumes an admissible minimizer. It constructs its
Stieltjes measure and an associated diffusion, proves
$\operatorname{supp}\mu_\gamma=[0,1)$ and strict increase of $\gamma$,
and obtains $\mathbb E u(t,X_t)^2=t$ and
$\mathbb E a(t,X_t)^2=1$ for every associated diffusion. The selected
formal statement has exactly this conditional scope; it does not assert a
smooth density.
Its [Lean implementation at the fixed source revision][support-main] implements the
[separately stated formal challenge][support-type]. The
[Comparator configuration][support-config] identifies the intended
comparison; the evidence retained with this draft does not establish
a successful research-target replay.

The second result concerns the scalar value. A bounded martingale ends
at a spin-valued random variable whose Brownian correlation represents
$P_*$. Finite Gaussian coefficients approximate that correlation at each
fixed $T<1$, followed by $T\uparrow1$. Its formal statement is separate
and retains the minimizer and diffusion hypotheses where needed. The QAOA
theorem goes further: for each requested accuracy it selects one finite
deterministic circuit, independent of size and disorder, whose limiting
expected energy approaches $P_*$. Neither formal statement asserts that
circuit conclusion.
The scalar clauses are in a [separate Lean implementation][value-main], with their
own [formal challenge][value-type] and [Comparator configuration][value-config].
Those links identify the selected statements, not a completed replay
receipt for either research target.

### 2.1 Structure of the argument The proof begins with regularity on strips bounded away from terminal time. It makes the diffusion $X$ and the gradient moment $q$ available, so a first variation can show where the minimizer is in contact. On a constant interval, the shape inequalities and the rational certificate give the strict curvature needed to contradict that contact. The zero-interval case uses a separate heat argument, and the possible terminal plateau needs its own exclusion. These steps lead to full support and the two moment equalities. In this manuscript route, the value argument then uses bounded-martingale convergence and the attained Parisi formula to express $P_*$ as a terminal Brownian correlation and an integral of expected curvature. Section 6 defines the terminal martingale variable and proves these equalities. The fixed-$T$ Gaussian approximation recovers this integral through Euler coupling, orthogonal normalization and mean-preserving rounding. The QAOA theorem additionally requires rooted energy identification, classical synthesis, removal of temporary seeds and transfer to fixed angles. The main route is §§3–5, then §§6–7, then §§8.1–8.6; §12 compares the two formal interfaces. The original analytic details are in [OpenAI (2026a), §§2–7][fs-main], and the circuit construction is in [OpenAI (2026b), §§2–6][q-intro]. The density theorem in §§9.1–9.2 is a further consequence of support and the PDE, not a premise of the scalar or circuit construction. The positive-temperature route in §11.1 independently supplies the same bounded classical input used for synthesis. The probability consequence in §11.2 requires a separate fixed-word second-moment theorem. These branches explain why the two selected formal statements are not a formal proof of the complete circuit theorem. These destinations separate premises of the support proof from its consequences. They locate the detailed arguments behind the short paper's support and density theorem. **The diffusion and moment identity.** For any admissible $\gamma$, the compact-strip estimates justify defining $X,q$ and computing $q'=\mathbb E a^2$; see [§2.4](#strip-estimates) and [§3.1](#gradient-moment). **Variational contact.** Minimality, admissible mass addition and compact mass removal give $G\ge0$, its vanishing on support and the contact slopes. The steps are in [§3.2](#feasible-variation), [§3.3](#measure-contact) and [§3.4](#contact-slopes). **Strict curvature.** Admissibility and a positive constant $c$ on an interval suffice; minimality is not needed. The shape comparisons, algebra and limiting argument are in [§4.3](#shape-comparisons), [§4.4](#curvature-algebra) and [§4.5](#plateau-limit). **Exclusion of gaps.** Combine contact with the appropriate positive, zero or terminal argument. The cases have separate destinations: [terminal](#terminal-gap), [bounded](#bounded-gaps) and [initial](#initial-gaps) gaps. **Positive density.** Full support comes first. Differentiated moments then give [smoothness in §9.1](#smooth-density-consequence), and a local comparison gives [strict positivity in §9.2](#positive-density). **Value and circuits.** Retain the same minimizer and diffusion through [the value identity in §6](#scalar-value-identities) and [the finite Gaussian construction in §7](#finite-gaussian-approximation). [The circuit argument in §8](#qaoa-construction) requires additional theorems. ### 2.2 The regularity available before the proof starts **Proposition 2.1 (compact-strip regularity).** For $\gamma\in\mathcal U$ and $0\le T<1$, the value has bounded, jointly continuous spatial derivatives of every positive finite order on $[0,T]\times\mathbb R$. If admissible coefficients converge in $L^1$ and their smooth, even, convex, one-Lipschitz terminal values converge uniformly to $|x|$, these spatial derivatives converge uniformly on each such strip. The bounds depend on the derivative order, the fixed strip and a common coefficient mass bound. Time derivatives need only exist almost everywhere across coefficient jumps. On an open constant interval, the heat formula supplies the additional time smoothness used in §4. The terminal estimate is $$ |x|\le\Phi_\gamma(t,x) \le |x|+\sqrt{2(1-t)/\pi}+\frac12\int_t^1\gamma(s)\,ds. $$ It controls approach to $|x|$ without differentiating that cusp. The strip estimates justify the interior calculations and finite meshes; the terminal bound and integrability justify the later endpoint limits. The two roles must remain separate. Their uses depend on the region and limit. On a fixed $[0,T]$ with $T<1$, bounded spatial derivatives and locally absolutely continuous time dependence justify the Itô identities and Euler coupling. Across a jump of $\gamma$, the spatial derivative moments remain continuous and the time equations hold almost everywhere; this is enough for contact slopes and the endpoint chord comparison. Inside a constant interval, classical time differentiation permits the strict-curvature calculation. As $T\uparrow1$, the controls change: the displayed value bound, integrable coefficient tails and martingale convergence justify first variation and terminal value. No differentiated estimate at the terminal cusp is used. These are [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 2.1 and its diffusion consequences][fs-reg]; [§2.4](#strip-estimates) reconstructs their uniformity. The hypotheses also have distinct uses. Zero field supplies evenness, $u(0,0)=0$ and reflection in the shape argument. The convention $\xi''=1$ fixes the curvature coefficients. Monotonicity gives bounded coefficients before time one and nonnegative coefficient jumps; it also turns a support gap into a constant interval. Integrability controls terminal tails and Fubini interchanges, while local finiteness of the Stieltjes measure is enough for compact mass removal. Minimality first enters through the variational inequality in §3; the constant-interval curvature estimate itself applies to an admissible coefficient without assuming it is a minimiser. [OpenAI (2026a), §§1–2][fs-main]; [OpenAI (2026a), §2][fs-reg]; [OpenAI (2026a), §6][fs-var]. ### 2.3 Which prior results play which role The imported ground-state formula supplies two facts with different uses. Auffinger and Chen's Theorem 1 identifies the ground-state limit with an infimum over $\mathcal U$. To choose a coefficient attaining that infimum, one must also use their construction in the proof of Lemma 3. In the cited arXiv v2, the theorem is on p. 3, the compactness construction is on pp. 7–9, and the lower-bound proof is on pp. 11–12. The support proof is conditional on a minimizer. From that hypothesis, continue directly with [the compact-strip estimates in §2.4](#strip-estimates). The construction below explains how attainment supplies the minimizer later used in the value and circuit arguments. Here is the part of that construction which supplies the witness. Let $\alpha_\beta$ be a positive-temperature Parisi distribution function. The source bounds $\beta\alpha_\beta(t)$ uniformly on each interval ending before one. Helly selection and a diagonal subsequence produce a nonnegative, nondecreasing right-continuous limit $\gamma_0$. In the SK normalization, the source's weighted integral bound also controls $\int_0^1\beta\alpha_\beta(t)\,dt$. For every nonnegative nondecreasing $h$, splitting at $1/2$ gives $\int_0^1 h(t)\,dt\le4\int_0^1t h(t)\,dt$: the first half is bounded by $h(1/2)/2$, and on the second half $t\ge1/2$. Fatou's lemma then gives $\gamma_0\in\mathcal U$. Mass can concentrate at time one during this limit, so compact convergence alone does not identify the limiting control problem. Write the limiting measure of the time coefficients as $$ \nu_0(dt)=\gamma_0(t)\,dt+m\delta_1(dt),\qquad m\geq0. $$ For an arbitrary admissible control, let $S$ denote its terminal state with coefficient $\gamma_0$. To see why the terminal choice is admissible, let the original control be $\alpha$ and put $S_s=B_s+\int_0^s\gamma_0(r)\alpha_r\,dr$. For a cutoff $\tau<1$ use $\alpha_s$ before $\tau$ and $g_k(S_s)$ afterwards, where $g_k$ is a continuous function bounded by one and converging pointwise to the sign with $\operatorname{sgn}(0)=1$. This control uses only information available at time $s$. At fixed $\tau,k$, first take the temperature limit; then let $\tau\uparrow1$ and $k\to\infty$. The continuous terminal evaluation has thereby approached $\operatorname{sgn}(S)$ without anticipating a future state. The endpoint atom then contributes $$ |S+m\operatorname{sgn}(S)|-|S|=m $$ to the reward and $$ \tfrac12m\bigl(\operatorname{sgn}(S)^2+1\bigr)=m $$ to the combined control and Parisi penalties. These contributions cancel. Taking the supremum over the remaining controls proves $P_*\geq\mathcal P(\gamma_0)$. The upper bound proved earlier in that paper gives $P_*\leq\inf_{\gamma\in\mathcal U}\mathcal P(\gamma)$. Therefore $$ P_*\leq\inf_{\gamma\in\mathcal U}\mathcal P(\gamma) \leq\mathcal P(\gamma_0)\leq P_*. $$ Thus $\gamma_0$ attains the infimum. The cancellation is a step in the imported existence proof; it is not an additional assumption about the Stieltjes measure $d\gamma_0$. In particular, $\nu_0$ here is the limit of coefficient-times-Lebesgue measures, not the order parameter's Stieltjes measure. The two measures must not be identified. [Auffinger and Chen, arXiv:1606.05335v2, pp. 7–12][ac17]. The cited theorem is stated for the almost-sure normalized maximum. Its expected-value formulation used here follows from Gaussian concentration. For $L_n=n^{-1}\max_\sigma H_n(\sigma)$, the Lipschitz constant in the Gaussian couplings is $\sqrt{(n-1)/(2n^2)}$. Hence $L_n-\mathbb E L_n\to0$ in probability. Since the almost-sure limit is the deterministic Parisi value, the deterministic sequence $\mathbb E L_n$ has the same limit. The full-support theorem below remains conditional on a minimizer; neither of the selected formal interfaces constructs one. [OpenAI full-support manuscript, Introduction, ground-state formula and its footnote][fs-main]. Auffinger–Chen–Zeng's infinite support does not exclude an interior gap. Their terminal-plateau observation anticipates one endpoint obstruction; the argument below supplies the quantitative boundary-layer proof used here. The full-support manuscript develops a rational coercivity route and credits Chen's 2026 theorem for the same full-support conclusion and smooth absolute continuity. Chen's Proposition 4.2 has the conditional crossing form $q''(t)=0\Rightarrow q'''(t)>0$; the cited rational certificate gives $q'''(t)>0$ throughout a positive constant interval. These are different sufficient mechanisms, and this record makes no priority claim for full support. [Auffinger, Chen and Zeng (2020), Theorem 1 and Remark 7][acz]; [Chen (2026), Theorem 1.3 and Proposition 4.2][chen2026]; [OpenAI (2026a), §§1–2][fs-main]. The transformed density comparisons also have antecedents in Lopatto's positive-temperature analysis and Chen's zero-temperature analysis; the rational coercive identity is the different step in the full-support proof. Zhou's positive-temperature interval-support result applies near the critical temperature, whereas Lopatto's cited theorem covers the low-temperature zero-field phase. Neither transfers full Stieltjes support to zero temperature on its own: for the minimizers, $\beta\mu_\beta$ converges vaguely on $[0,1)$ to the zero-temperature Stieltjes measure, while the unscaled Parisi probability measures converge weakly on $[0,1]$ to $\delta_1$. These are different measures and topologies. Convergence without an interval-specific lower bound can lose support information. The direct zero-temperature gap proof below is therefore essential. [Chen (2026), Remarks 1.4–1.5][chen2026]; [OpenAI (2026a), §§1–2][fs-main]. The coefficient classes in this comparison can be translated explicitly. In the positive-temperature convention, write $$ U_t=-\frac{\beta^2}{2}(U_{yy}+\alpha_\nu U_y^2), \qquad U(1,y)=\log\cosh y. $$ Set $\Phi_\beta(t,x)=\beta^{-1}U(t,\beta x)$ and $\gamma_\beta=\beta\alpha_\nu$. Direct differentiation gives $$ (\Phi_\beta)_t=-\tfrac12\bigl((\Phi_\beta)_{xx} +\gamma_\beta(\Phi_\beta)_x^2\bigr),\qquad \Phi_\beta(1,x)=\beta^{-1}\log\cosh(\beta x). $$ Dividing the associated diffusion by $\beta$ likewise gives unit Brownian noise and drift $\gamma_\beta(\Phi_\beta)_x$. Conversely, every bounded nonnegative, nondecreasing, right-continuous coefficient on $[0,1)$ has this form: choose $\beta>0$ at least its supremum, take distribution function $\alpha_\nu=\gamma/\beta$ below one, and put the remaining probability mass at one. This identifies coefficient classes, not minimizers at different temperatures. The terminal values differ from $|x|$ by at most $(\log2)/\beta$, but passing a strict inequality to the cusp and to coefficients unbounded near one still needs uniform estimates. A qualitative crossing statement alone supplies no positive limiting fourth-moment margin. [Lopatto, arXiv:2607.11756v4, equation (1.2), §2 and Proposition 5.1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11756v4). Two related works sharpen the comparison without entering the pinned September proof. [Lopatto, arXiv:2607.11756v4, Proposition 5.1 and (5.8)–Corollary 5.6](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11756v4), proves a conditional curvature crossing on a positive constant interval. Its integrating factor makes a transformed curvature derivative strictly increasing, so the associated contact derivative decreases and then increases; it does not assert an unconditional positive third derivative. [Lopatto, arXiv:2610.00127v1, Theorem 2.3 and §8](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00127v1), works at positive temperature and positive external field. Its comparison requires one-sided bounds on the coefficient before and after the chosen time, a moment inequality and a stationarity equality. Several of these conditions are automatic in its density application: monotonicity supplies the one-sided bounds at a continuity point, contact on a full-support interval makes the scalar inequality an equality, and the quotient formula for the coefficient supplies stationarity. Its moment bootstrap then gives smooth, strictly positive density on a nontrivial support interval; a singleton support is a separate case. Appendix B, Theorem B.1 and equation (B.1), also prove strict positivity in the zero-field positive-temperature setting, where the extra noncentered-law condition is unnecessary. These results are therefore close analytic antecedents. The distinction used below is the unconditional quantitative fourth-moment margin for the comparison coefficient and its controlled passage to the zero-temperature cusp. Here is an explicit example of the information lost in such a limit. It concerns admissible measures, not Parisi minimizers. Put $g=\mathbf1_{[0,1/3]\cup[2/3,1)}$ and $q_n=1-n^{-2}$, and for $n\ge2$ define $$ \mu_n(dt)=\frac{g(t)+n^{-1}}n\mathbf1_{[0,q_n]}(t)\,dt +\left(1-\frac1n\int_0^{q_n}(g(t)+n^{-1})\,dt\right)\delta_{q_n}(dt). $$ The continuous part has mass at most $(2/3+1/n)/n<1$, so these are probability measures with a positive endpoint atom. Their density is positive throughout $[0,q_n]$, giving $\operatorname{supp}\mu_n=[0,q_n]$. Their continuous mass tends to zero and $q_n\to1$, hence $\mu_n\Rightarrow\delta_1$ weakly on $[0,1]$. For a compactly supported continuous test function on $[0,1)$, the endpoint atom eventually lies outside its support. Consequently $n\mu_n\to g(t)\,dt$ vaguely there, although the limit vanishes on $(1/3,2/3)$. Even the cumulative coefficients converge in the topology used for the PDE: with $\gamma_n(t)=n\mu_n([0,t])$ and $\gamma(t)=\int_0^t g(s)\,ds$, their difference is $t/n$ below $q_n$, and $\gamma_n=n$ on the terminal strip of length $n^{-2}$. Thus $$ \|\gamma_n-\gamma\|_{L^1(0,1)}\le\frac1{2n}+\frac1n\longrightarrow0. $$ Every $\gamma_n$ is admissible, but $d\gamma$ has an interior gap. Minimality and the gap argument supply information that these convergences alone do not. An atom added at time one is likewise invisible to the coefficient on $[0,1)$ and hence to its PDE and variational functional; the zero-temperature problem does not select an endpoint mass. Control and gradient-martingale methods have antecedents in [Auffinger–Chen](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00220-014-2254-z) and [Jagannath–Tobasco](https://arxiv.org/abs/1502.04398v4). A finite-temperature theorem with smooth terminal value $\log\cosh$ does not alone establish the result with terminal cusp $|x|$. The required compact-strip and terminal estimates are supplied in [OpenAI (2026a), §2][fs-reg]; [Chen–Handschy–Lerman](https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.04368v4) supplies earlier zero-temperature regularity, control and uniqueness results (Theorem 4 for uniqueness). This is distinct from the earlier finite-temperature uniqueness result of Auffinger and Chen. [Montanari](https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.10897v2) and [El Alaoui–Montanari–Sellke](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.00904v1) inform normalised discretisation and optimisation. **Proposition 3.1 (variational contact).** For an admissible minimizer, the potential $G(s)=\int_s^1(q(t)-t)\,dt$ is nonnegative on $[0,1)$ and vanishes on $S=\operatorname{supp}\mu_\gamma$. At every $s\in S$, $q(s)=s$ and $q'(s)\le1$, with a right derivative at zero. The minimisation takes place over nonnegative Stieltjes measures with an integrable cumulative function. Their total mass is free. We first derive the variation of the functional, then use changes of measure which preserve this admissible class. The result will be contact on the *existing* support; the exclusion of gaps comes afterwards. ### 3.1 The moment function before minimisation Fix any $\gamma\in\mathcal U$, without yet assuming that it minimises $\mathcal P$. Compact-strip regularity and Itô's formula give $$ u(t,X_t)=\int_0^t a(s,X_s)\,dB_s,\qquad q(t):=\mathbb E u(t,X_t)^2 =\int_0^t\mathbb E a(s,X_s)^2\,ds. $$ The initial term vanishes because zero field makes $\Phi$ even and $u(0,0)=0$. Thus $q(0)=0$, $0\le q(t)\le1$, and $$ q'(t)=\mathbb E a(t,X_t)^2\qquad(0\le t<1), $$ with a right derivative at zero. The integrand is continuous on each compact time strip, so $q\in C^1[0,1)$. These facts hold for every admissible coefficient. They do not yet say that $q(t)=t$. The source proves them by smooth approximation on $[0,T]$, $T<1$; it never differentiates the terminal cusp $|x|$ at time one. [OpenAI (2026a), Lemmas 2.1–2.2][fs-reg]. ### 3.2 The feasible right derivative Let $\eta\in L^1(0,1)$ and suppose that $\gamma+\varepsilon\eta\in\mathcal U$ for $0\le\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_0$, where $\varepsilon_0>0$. This is a feasibility hypothesis: an arbitrary signed bump in $\gamma$ need not preserve monotonicity. Since $\mathcal U$ is convex, it is enough to check that the endpoint $\gamma+\varepsilon_0\eta$ is admissible. The formula below is the zero-field, $\xi''=1$ specialization of [Chen, Handschy and Lerman, arXiv:1609.04368v4, Proposition 4](https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.04368v4). Their chord $\gamma_\theta=(1-\theta)\gamma+\theta\gamma_1$ gives this direction by taking $\gamma_1=\gamma+\varepsilon_0\eta$ and $\theta=\varepsilon/\varepsilon_0$. Their class $\mathcal U$ permits unnormalized cumulative measures with finite cumulative integral, so this change of parameter also covers the scaling direction $-\gamma$. We reconstruct the detailed PDE proof from OpenAI's Lemma 6.1. For $0<\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_0$, put $\beta=\gamma+\varepsilon\eta$, $\widetilde u=\Phi_{\beta,x}$ and $D=\Phi_\beta-\Phi_\gamma$. Subtracting the two PDEs gives $$ D_t=-\frac12D_{xx} -\frac12\beta(\widetilde u+u)D_x -\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\eta u^2. $$ The choice of diffusion $$ dY_t^\varepsilon =\frac12\beta(t)(\widetilde u+u)(t,Y_t^\varepsilon)\,dt+dB_t, \qquad Y_0^\varepsilon=0, $$ cancels the first-order spatial term when Itô's formula is applied to $D(t,Y_t^\varepsilon)$. Its drift has absolute value at most $\beta(t)$, which is integrable. On $[0,T]$ the resulting identity is $$ D(0,0)=\mathbb E D(T,Y_T^\varepsilon) +\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\int_0^T \eta(t)\mathbb E[u(t,Y_t^\varepsilon)^2]\,dt. $$ At coefficient jumps the time derivatives need only exist almost everywhere. The source obtains this identity by approximating both coefficients by monotone step functions with the same smooth terminal datum, and then passing to the limit using the compact-strip estimates. The control representation, applied with the same control on each side, gives the time-local difference bound $$ \sup_x|D(T,x)|\le\frac{3\varepsilon}{2} \int_T^1|\eta(t)|\,dt. $$ Hence $T\uparrow1$, at fixed $\varepsilon$, removes the terminal term even after division by $\varepsilon$. We obtain the exact finite-change identity $$ \frac{\Phi_{\gamma+\varepsilon\eta}(0,0)-\Phi_\gamma(0,0)} {\varepsilon} =\frac12\int_0^1\eta(t) \mathbb E[u(t,Y_t^\varepsilon)^2]\,dt. $$ As $\varepsilon\downarrow0$, the coefficients converge in $L^1$ and have uniformly bounded $L^1$ norms. On each fixed strip, their gradients converge uniformly and have common spatial Lipschitz bounds. Coupling with the same Brownian motion and applying Gronwall's inequality therefore gives $Y^\varepsilon\to X$ uniformly on that strip. The integrand converges to $\eta(t)q(t)$ for each $t<1$, and its absolute value is at most $|\eta(t)|$. Dominated convergence, followed by subtraction of the linear Parisi penalty, now yields $$ D_+\mathcal P(\gamma)[\eta] :=\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0} \frac{\mathcal P(\gamma+\varepsilon\eta)-\mathcal P(\gamma)} {\varepsilon} =\frac12\int_0^1\eta(t)(q(t)-t)\,dt. $$ If $\gamma$ is a minimiser, this derivative is nonnegative for every feasible direction. It need not vanish: the minimisation has one-sided constraints. [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 6.1, equations (6.1)–(6.2)][fs-var]. ### 3.3 Which changes of measure are allowed? Write $\mu=\mu_\gamma$ and $S=\operatorname{supp}\mu$, with support relative to $[0,1)$. Tonelli's theorem gives the useful identity $$ \int_0^1\gamma(t)\,dt =\int_{[0,1)}\!\int_s^1dt\,\mu(ds) =\int_{[0,1)}(1-s)\,\mu(ds)<\infty. $$ This is weighted finiteness, not a bound on $\mu([0,1))$. In particular, there is no normalisation constraint requiring mass added at one point to be removed elsewhere. Define the tail potential $$ G(s)=\int_s^1(q(t)-t)\,dt\qquad(0\le s<1). $$ It is continuous, satisfies $|G(s)|\le1-s$, and has $G'(s)=s-q(s)$ and $G''(s)=1-q'(s)$ on compact strips, with one-sided interpretations at zero. The following two competitors suffice. | Change to the Stieltjes measure | Direction in the cumulative function | Allowed parameter | Consequence at a minimiser | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Add $\varepsilon\delta_s$, $0\le s<1$ | $\eta(t)=\mathbf1_{[s,1)}(t)$ | $\varepsilon\ge0$ | $G(s)\ge0$ | | Remove $\varepsilon\nu$, where $\nu=\mu|_K$ and $K\subset[0,1)$ is compact | $\eta_K(t)=-\nu([0,t])$ | $0\le\varepsilon\le1$ | $\int_KG(s)\,\mu(ds)\le0$ | For atom addition, the new cumulative function is nonnegative, nondecreasing and right-continuous. Its integral increases by $\varepsilon(1-s)$, so it remains in $\mathcal U$. This includes $s=0$: an atom there adds a constant to $\gamma$ on all of $[0,1)$. The point $1$ is outside the measure's domain and is not an additional competitor. The derivative formula gives $D_+\mathcal P(\gamma)[\mathbf1_{[s,1)}]=G(s)/2$, proving $G\ge0$ everywhere below one. For removal, choose $T<1$ with $K\subset[0,T]$. Then $\nu(K)\le\gamma(T)<\infty$. The measure $\mu-\varepsilon\nu$ is nonnegative for $0\le\varepsilon\le1$, so its cumulative function is nonnegative, nondecreasing and right-continuous. It lies between zero and $\gamma$, hence is integrable; also $|\eta_K|\le\nu(K)$. **Abstract.** The Stieltjes measure of every integrable minimiser of the
zero-temperature Parisi functional for the pure, zero-field
Sherrington–Kirkpatrick model has full support on $[0,1)$ and a smooth
density that is strictly positive on $(0,1)$. We reconstruct OpenAI's quantitative
argument, organised around two uses of one spatial-moment inequality.
On a positive constant interval, it makes the derivative of the gradient
second moment strictly convex, contradicting the endpoint conditions
imposed by minimality. The same curvature and the bounded gradient
also exclude terminal gaps. Full support then gives moment identities and
smoothness; a local constant replacement transfers the inequality to the minimiser and
forces its density to be positive. H.-B. Chen previously proved full support
and smooth nonnegative density. We isolate the fixed-time spatial moment
and the positive margin that survives local replacement, while importing its
shape comparisons and full polynomial identity. We also derive the scalar value
identity and explain its classical optimisation consequence. For the quantum approximate
optimization algorithm (QAOA), we identify the rooted energy of a finite Gaussian
observable and the separate circuit theorem that approximates it. A further
second-moment theorem gives a measured near-optimal configuration on the same
random instance, with the circuit word fixed before the number of spins grows.

For independent standard Gaussian couplings $J_{ij}$, the pure,
zero-field [Sherrington–Kirkpatrick (SK) Hamiltonian][SK] is
$$
H_n(\sigma)=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i<j}J_{ij}\sigma_i\sigma_j,
\qquad \sigma\in\{-1,1\}^n.
$$
The limiting ground-state energy per spin, with the maximisation
convention, is
$$
P_*:=\lim_{n\to\infty}n^{-1}\mathbb E\max_\sigma H_n(\sigma).
$$
The Parisi formula expresses $P_*$ as a minimum over nondecreasing
functions. Our subject is the structure of a minimiser: its increments
charge every interval of overlap scales below one, and in fact have
strictly positive density at each interior scale. The proof uses one
quantitative bound twice, first to exclude constant intervals and then,
after an approximation, to prove pointwise positivity.

For two configurations, their overlap is
$R(\sigma,\tau)=n^{-1}\sum_i\sigma_i\tau_i$. It determines the
energy covariance: $\mathbb E[H_n(\sigma)H_n(\tau)]=nR^2/2-1/2$.
Thus the Gaussian law of the energies is encoded by the overlaps.
We use the covariance convention $\xi(t)=t^2/2$, so $\xi''=1$;
adding one independent centred Gaussian of
variance $1/2$ to every configuration's energy gives covariance
$n\xi(R)$ and leaves the expected maximum unchanged. This is the
normalisation of the ground-state Parisi formula of
[Auffinger and Chen (2017), Theorem 1][AC]. There are no higher-order
interactions and no external field.

Let $\mathcal U$ consist of the nonnegative, nondecreasing,
right-continuous functions $\gamma:[0,1)\to[0,\infty)$ satisfying
$\int_0^1\gamma(t)\,dt<\infty$. Define the locally finite Stieltjes
measure by
$$
\mu_\gamma([0,t])=\gamma(t),\qquad 0\leq t<1.
$$
Thus $\mu_\gamma((s,t])=\gamma(t)-\gamma(s)$: the measure records
the increments of $\gamma$. A point mass (atom) of size $\gamma(0)$
is allowed at zero, and the total mass need not be finite or equal

A support gap is a relatively open interval of positive length with
zero mass; the cumulative coefficient is constant on such an interval.

The Parisi functional $\mathcal P(\gamma)$ is defined using an
auxiliary value function $\Phi_\gamma(t,x)$, where $x\in\mathbb R$
is a spatial variable and $t$ is the overlap parameter, treated as
time in the equation. Write $\Phi=\Phi_\gamma$ and use subscripts
for partial derivatives. The backward equation, terminal condition
and functional are
$$
\Phi_t=-\tfrac12\bigl(\Phi_{xx}+\gamma(t)\Phi_x^2\bigr),
\qquad \Phi(1,x)=|x|,
\qquad
\mathcal P(\gamma)=\Phi_\gamma(0,0)-\tfrac12\int_0^1t\gamma(t)\,dt.
$$
The terminal value $|x|$ is the zero-temperature value of one spin
in a field $x$. For an integrable
coefficient, the PDE solution is interpreted by approximation from
bounded monotone coefficients. The exact control
definition and stability theorem are [OpenAI (2026a), §1 and
Lemmas 2.1–2.2][FS]. To turn minimality of $\mathcal P$ into a
condition on $\gamma$, we use a random process whose gradient moment
measures the first-order cost of changing $\gamma$. Write $u=\Phi_x$ for the spatial gradient
and $a=\Phi_{xx}$ for its spatial derivative. Let $B$ be standard

$$
dX_t=\gamma(t)u(t,X_t)\,dt+dB_t,\qquad X_0=0,

minimality will force $q(t)=t$ on the support of $\mu_\gamma$.
